description: Reader-facing micro-wiki for lightly mentioned historical people, families, clans, factions, institutions, events and named historical works. The novel provides the trigger and reading context; an authoritative external historical source provides a concise historical explanation.

source_policy.novel_trigger_source: Canonical local chapter corpus under data/source/book1 and data/source/book2
source_policy.rule: Never merge external historical facts into novel evidence.

novel_trigger.context: Why the reference matters at this point

wiki.summary: Two or three concise lines of salient historical context.

novel_trigger.context: Historical commander whose actions at Sekigahara are described in the opening scene.

wiki.summary: Daimyo who commanded a major contingent at Sekigahara. His decision to switch allegiance to Tokugawa Ieyasu was a decisive factor in the Eastern Army's victory.

source.title: Kobayakawa Hideaki Route
source.publisher: Gifu Sekigahara Battlefield Memorial Museum / Gifu Prefecture

novel_trigger.context: Principal Western Army commander named in the opening description of Sekigahara.

wiki.summary: Toyotomi administrator and leading commander of the Western Army at Sekigahara. He opposed Tokugawa Ieyasu and was defeated at the battle that established Tokugawa supremacy.

source.title: Ishida Mitsunari Route
source.publisher: Gifu Sekigahara Battlefield Memorial Museum / Gifu Prefecture

novel_trigger.context: Major Western Army commander named among the defeated commanders at Sekigahara.

wiki.summary: Major Toyotomi ally who commanded the largest Western Army contingent at Sekigahara. His forces fought in the main battle against the Tokugawa-led coalition.

source.title: Fukushima Masanori Route — Ukita Hideie’s Encampment
source.publisher: Gifu Sekigahara Battlefield Memorial Museum / Gifu Prefecture

novel_trigger.context: Western Army commander named among the forces defeated at Sekigahara.

wiki.summary: Daimyo of Satsuma who commanded the Shimazu contingent at Sekigahara. After the Western Army collapsed, he fought his way through the opposing ranks and returned to Satsuma.

source.title: Ishida Mitsunari Route — Shimazu Yoshihiro’s Encampment
source.publisher: Gifu Sekigahara Battlefield Memorial Museum / Gifu Prefecture

novel_trigger.context: Western Army commander named among the defeated commanders at Sekigahara.

wiki.summary: Commander of a Western Army contingent at Sekigahara. After the Western Army was routed, Konishi fled, surrendered, and was executed in Kyoto together with Ishida Mitsunari.

source.title: Kuroda Nagamasa Route — Konishi Yukinaga’s Encampment
source.publisher: Gifu Sekigahara Battlefield Memorial Museum / Gifu Prefecture

novel_trigger.context: Leader of the victorious Eastern coalition identified in the opening aftermath of Sekigahara.

wiki.summary: Leader of the Eastern coalition at Sekigahara and the central figure in the Tokugawa victory. His triumph over the Western coalition established Tokugawa political dominance in Japan.

source.title: Tokugawa Ieyasu Route
source.publisher: Gifu Sekigahara Battlefield Memorial Museum / Gifu Prefecture

novel_trigger.context: The battle whose immediate aftermath forms the opening setting of Book I.

wiki.summary: The decisive 1600 battle between the Tokugawa-led coalition and the forces aligned with the Toyotomi cause. The victory shifted the balance of power decisively toward Tokugawa Ieyasu.

source.title: About the Gifu Sekigahara Battlefield Memorial Museum
source.publisher: Gifu Sekigahara Battlefield Memorial Museum / Gifu Prefecture

novel_trigger.context: Victorious coalition at Sekigahara.

wiki.summary: Modern shorthand for the coalition led by Tokugawa Ieyasu at Sekigahara. The Gifu museum notes that these 'Eastern' and 'Western' labels were not actually used at the time of the battle.

source.title: About the Gifu Sekigahara Battlefield Memorial Museum
source.publisher: Gifu Sekigahara Battlefield Memorial Museum / Gifu Prefecture

novel_trigger.context: Defeated coalition at Sekigahara.

wiki.summary: Modern shorthand for the coalition opposing Tokugawa Ieyasu at Sekigahara and associated with the Toyotomi cause. The label is useful for readers, although it was not the period's own terminology.

source.title: About the Gifu Sekigahara Battlefield Memorial Museum
source.publisher: Gifu Sekigahara Battlefield Memorial Museum / Gifu Prefecture

novel_trigger.context: The novel states that the Hon'iden and Shimmen families trace their lineage to the Akamatsu house.

wiki.summary: A major samurai house of Harima that rose to prominence as shugo-daimyo during the Muromachi period. The Hyogo Prefectural Museum of History documents the clan's long political and military presence in western Harima.

novel_trigger.context: Takuan recalls the legend of Hiromasa playing the flute at the Suzaku Gate in Kyoto.

wiki.summary: A Heian-period court noble and celebrated gagaku musician (918–980), especially known as a master of wind instruments. The National Theatre of Japan records him as the compiler of the 966 flute notation collection known as Hakuga's flute score.

source.title: The lives of gagaku musicians — Heian period

context_source.title: The Story of Minamoto no Hiromasa and the Demon's Flute

novel_trigger.context: Lord Ikeda explains the Shimmen family's historical connection to the Akamatsu lineage and names Masanori in that genealogy.

wiki.summary: Akamatsu Masanori (1455–1496) was a medieval military lord and shugo who restored the Akamatsu family's position in Harima, Bizen and Mimasaka. He died in 1496, after which the family passed to his adopted heir Yoshimura.

novel_trigger.context: The chapter title and Takuan's discussion invoke Sunzi's Art of War as a framework for strategy and conduct.

wiki.summary: An ancient Chinese military treatise traditionally attributed to Sunzi (Sun Tzu). Its exact composition date is debated, but it is generally associated with the late Warring States / early classical military tradition.

novel_trigger.context: The opening of Book II uses Nobunaga's career and death to frame Kyoto's recent political past.

wiki.summary: Japanese military leader (1534–1582) whose campaigns transformed the late Sengoku political order. The authority source fixes identity and dates; the novel's interpretation remains literary context.

novel_trigger.context: Book II's opening chronology names Hideyoshi as Nobunaga's successor and as the predecessor to Tokugawa supremacy.

wiki.summary: Japanese ruler (1536–1598) who held the office of kanpaku. The institutional authority record also preserves Hashiba Hideyoshi among his variant names.

novel_trigger.context: The political introduction states that Ieyasu transferred the shogunal title to his third son Hidetada.

wiki.summary: Second Tokugawa shogun (1579–1632), son of Tokugawa Ieyasu. This historical identification does not validate the novel's broader political narration.

novel_trigger.context: Book II names Hideyori at Osaka Castle while explaining the unsettled Tokugawa–Toyotomi balance.

wiki.summary: Son and heir of Toyotomi Hideyoshi (1593–1615), associated with Osaka Castle and the final Toyotomi resistance. Only this general identity is supplied as context.

novel_trigger.context: Seijūrō and his companions discuss attending the popular Okuni performance in Kyoto.

wiki.summary: At the start of the seventeenth century, a woman calling herself an Izumo shrine maiden, Okuni, made kabuki-odori highly popular in Kyoto; the form used song, dance and the fashions of kabukimono.

source.title: The Beginning — History of Kabuki
source.publisher: National Theatre of Japan / Japan Arts Council

novel_trigger.context: Travelers describe the retired Yagyū master at Koyagyū before he later enters the narrative physically.

wiki.summary: Nara City's historical material identifies Yagyū Munetoshi (Sekishūsai, 1527–1606) as a leading Yagyū figure and links his tradition with Kamiizumi Nobutsuna. The novel's meetings and dialogue are not treated as documentary history.

novel_trigger.context: Travelers identify Munenori as Sekishūsai's heir and report that he is away in Edo; this remains a mention, not physical presence.

wiki.summary: Nara City's guide identifies Munenori as Sekishūsai's fifth son, a servant of Tokugawa Ieyasu and sword instructor to the second and third shoguns; he later became the first Yagyū daimyo.

novel_trigger.context: Musashi visits the Hōzōin establishment and confronts its spear tradition.

wiki.summary: A Japanese spear tradition whose official lineage identifies the monk Hōzōin Kakuzenbō Hōin In'ei as founder. The historical school does not authenticate the novel's individual bouts.

novel_trigger.context: Book II names the master associated with In'ei and Yagyū Muneyoshi; the translation's Kōizumi is normalized cautiously to the historically documented Kamiizumi tradition.

wiki.summary: Sword master Kamiizumi Nobutsuna, also styled Ise-no-kami, is linked in Nara City's Yagyū historical material with Sekishūsai. The novel's translated name and anecdotes remain literary evidence.
